text: A British consul with no real consulate left drinks his way through a single day in a small Mexican town in 1939. Outside, the streets are filling for the Day of the Dead; further off, Europe is going to war, and the two facts keep brushing against each other without quite meeting. Geoffrey Firmin's ex-wife Yvonne has come back with a plan for repair, and his half-brother Hugh, who believes in causes, keeps looking for the sentence that will land. Huston allows 112 minutes and one calendar day: no reprieve of a time jump, no second morning on which to try again. The hold of the thing is how ordinary the mechanics stay - a drink ordered, a car hired, a conversation joined in the middle. Rescue arrives with its bags packed and finds very little to take hold of.

Twenty-two chapters of Genesis, 175 minutes, and the film gets no further than Abraham. What follows is not a story but a sequence of separate weathers: a garden, a killing in a field, a flood, a covenant made with an old man in the desert. Nothing carries across except God, and the practical questions keep surfacing - how to photograph a world with nothing in it yet, how many animals are enough, what a man looks like building a boat for years while the neighbours watch. It is an Italian production spoken in English, pitched at a scale that assumes an audience willing to sit still. The Cain and Abel passage is the hardest and the least decorated: two brothers, a field, nobody else alive to appeal to. Size is what the film advertises. Patience is what it actually asks for.

Kidnapping is a business with overheads: the captives have to be fed, watched, and kept breathing until somebody pays. Three outlaws take a former ranch foreman and an heiress, and the arithmetic of that arrangement is the whole picture. Once the abduction is done nobody can leave, so the western's usual motion - riding somewhere - gives way to waiting, and waiting turns into conversation between men who may well have to kill each other. Boetticher works in dry country with a cast small enough to count on one hand, and he is unsentimental about the fact that the woman is a sum of money to everyone present. Seventy-eight minutes, cut to sit at the bottom of a bill, and not a minute of it idles. The National Film Registry has it, which is a strange fate for a programme filler.

Tod Hackett paints backdrops for a studio, work that only has to convince from one angle. Around him, 1930s Los Angeles is full of people who came for a career and stayed for the weather: the aspiring actress next door, Faye Greener, who has worked out that a quiet accountant named Homer Simpson is the safer arrangement, and a floating population of extras waiting on a call. Schlesinger takes 145 minutes over this, and the length is the method - the film accumulates rather than advances, letting boarding houses, back lots and crowds fill in until the city has a temperature. It was built to be looked at, and its Academy Award for cinematography registers as much. What holds early on is smaller: the courtesy with which everyone lies about how well things are going.

The accusation comes from a prison ward. A wounded hoodlum says the doctor treating him killed his brother, and race is the whole of his reasoning - 1950, and Hollywood was not often this direct about it. Mankiewicz builds the case out of hospital procedure: charts, a request for an autopsy, the chain of permission a young Black physician has to climb before he is believed about his own work. The corridor does what a courtroom would do elsewhere. The hatred is not staged as an aberration in an otherwise sound arrangement; it has friends, addresses, a neighbourhood ready to act on it. The screenplay's Academy Award is worth mentioning for one reason: the writing gives the bigot a coherence of his own instead of the incoherence that would let everybody else off.

Filmed and released while the war in it was still being fought, so nobody on screen knows how any of it ends. Peter Davis borrows a phrase Lyndon B. Johnson used often - that victory would come from winning the hearts and minds of the Vietnamese - and turns it against the men who said it, cutting from officers speaking evenly in quiet rooms to what those sentences describe on the ground. The method is juxtaposition, and it is not fair; the unfairness is the argument. It took the Academy Award for documentary feature. What holds now is less the polemic than the interviews: American commanders, William C. Westmoreland among them, and Vietnamese civilians, each given long enough on camera to say more than they intended. Nothing is retrospective. The war is present tense, and the film has no idea it is history.

The star pitcher and the least essential catcher on a New York club are friends, which in professional sport is rarely a symmetrical arrangement. Henry Wiggen is good enough to make demands; Bruce Pearson is not good enough to make any, and over one season he becomes the thing Henry bends his contract and his temper around. Nobody plays it as tragedy. The register is clubhouse comedy - card games, hazing, bus rides, the manufactured boredom of a long schedule - and the illness sits underneath it like weather that has not arrived. What makes the film work is structural rather than sentimental: the season keeps going. Games are played, the standings move, and what the two men know has to be fitted around a calendar that was never going to pause.

Being laughed at without knowing it is difficult to play for laughs without turning cruel. That is the problem this 1925 comedy sets itself: a freshman who is neither athletic nor graceful, and unaware of how his mannerisms land, arrives on campus determined to be liked and settles on the football team as the route. The audience is ahead of him from the first minute. Silent comedy often solves such things with speed; seventy-seven minutes leaves room for the slower kind of embarrassment, the kind that has to be watched developing. College football was a mass enthusiasm in America by then, which is why a practice field can be shot with the gravity of a stadium. The National Film Registry keeps it. The humiliation is what still stings, and it is played straight enough that the laughs arrive faintly ashamed of themselves.

An out-of-work American showgirl arrives in Paris with no money and one usable skill: people believe her. The title she invents for herself is Hungarian, far enough away to be awkward to check, and the comedy runs on the discovery that high society is a system of assumptions rather than verifications. Everyone at the table is performing something; hers is only the newest performance. Ninety-four minutes, 1939, and the pace is set by the need never to be alone long enough to be questioned. The world of the film is dinner tables and borrowed evening clothes, where the dress licenses the claim. The pleasure is procedural - watching a lie get maintained under load is a species of suspense, and Leisen plays it that way, with the timing of a thriller and none of the anxiety.

Everything after the opening is flight: a man on foot in a city that has decided to find him, kept ahead of it by people who owe him nothing and hide him anyway - the neighbourhood he came up in and, improbably, some disaffected Hells Angels. The trigger comes early, when he steps in while police are working over a Black Panther, and from there the film drops the shape a crime picture is supposed to have. Van Peebles made it in 1971 outside the studios, and the roughness reads as a position rather than an accident. The scores it still draws are low and unsettled, which is what happens to a film never built to be liked by everyone watching. The National Film Registry took it regardless. The justification is the logistics of concealment: how many small decisions it takes to keep one man out of sight.

A cornerstone comes out of a condemned building and there is a frog inside it, and the frog can sing. The rest is a machine for ruining one man's life, and it runs seven minutes. He has proof in a box; the proof will only perform in private. Each attempt to convert the miracle into money - an agent, a theatre, the life savings - meets the same flat croak at the same wrong instant, and the repetition has the patience of a fable rather than the pace of a gag reel. Chuck Jones times it so the audience is always a beat ahead of the man and never ahead of the frog. The National Film Registry lists it among features at a seventh of their length. What keeps it upright is that nothing is ever explained: the frog's origin, its taste in songs, its motive, if it has one.

Long Beach, California, 1979: one man on a stage at the Terrace Theatre and a crew whose only job is to stay out of the way. Concert films usually pad - backstage footage, crowd montage, the tour as narrative. This one keeps the camera on Richard Pryor and lets the material run: race, sex, family, and above all himself, treated with less mercy than any of the others, while the audience stays audible throughout and changes what the timing has to do. The restraint is the direction. Live comedy lives in pauses and recoveries, and those survive only if the cutting leaves them alone. It sits on the National Film Registry, which for a filmed stand-up set means somebody decided the performance was itself the film. Seventy-eight minutes, one room, and no cutaway available if the room turns.

In 1925 an audience could be shown a living dinosaur and had almost no way of working out how it had been done. That gap drives this first adaptation of Arthur Conan Doyle's novel: an expedition, a plateau where prehistoric animals have gone on existing, and a great deal of screen time given to those animals merely being - feeding, fighting, crossing a landscape with no human in the frame. The story around them is standard adventure business, romance included, and its job is to justify the trip. What has lasted is the patience of the effects work, which photographs the creatures as wildlife rather than as exhibits, and the National Film Registry entry is as much for the method as for the picture. A hundred and four minutes was a large bet on a trick nobody had yet seen sustained.

An infected wound, a camp below Kilimanjaro, and a writer with nothing left to do but go back over things. Harry Street stays more or less still for the length of the film; the picture moves instead, backward through the life he assembled and the work he made of it, which puts nearly all the weight on how one memory is joined to the next. It is 1952 and in colour, made to be looked at - the Academy's award for colour cinematography is legible in most of the exteriors. Adventure is the genre label. The actual business is a man auditing his own choices with a fever on, and the odd, effective thing about it is the stillness at the centre: almost nothing happens in the present tense, and the film has to live on the quality of the remembering.
